title: When the Roadmap Meets Real Capacity
summary: A roadmap only helps once it survives a talk about real capacity. Count the hidden work, keep priority apart from order, say no cleanly and check the plan every week.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
On the wall, the roadmap looks fine. Every card has a name, a quarter and a color, and the whole thing feels tidy. Then Monday shows up with two production issues, one person on leave, a vendor running late, and a feature that turns out to need a data migration nobody counted. The roadmap hasn't become useless. It has just met the actual week.

This is where a lot of teams get stuck. Everyone looks at the same board and hears something different. Product hears "delay". Engineering hears "pressure". QA hears "the risk lands on us at the end". Leadership hears "we don't know". The conversation gets tense fast, and it's rarely because anyone is acting in bad faith.

A roadmap works best as a tool for choosing: what matters most, what can move, what must not get squeezed, and what you're giving up to make room. If one honest conversation about capacity knocks the whole plan over, it was mostly decoration. Here's a way to have that conversation without it turning into a blame session.

Count the capacity you actually have

Start by putting the invisible work on the table, in plain words. Story points and velocity only cover the work that made it onto tickets. A real week also holds support requests, code review, discovery, deep testing, release coordination, meetings, onboarding a new teammate, incidents, and the cost of switching between all of the above.

This isn't a soft complaint. Google's SRE book says their SRE organization aims to keep operational work below 50% of each SRE's time, and that quarterly surveys put the average at about 33% (Eliminating Toil). That's a team whose job includes operations, so your number will differ. The lesson carries over anyway: run-the-service work is big enough that a well-run org measures it and puts a ceiling on it.

A quick worked example helps. These numbers are made up, so swap in your own:

Two-week sprint, team of five Person-days
On paper: 5 people × 10 days50
Leave, added up across the team−4
On-call and support rotation (one person, half time)−5
Code review, roughly an hour a day each−6
Planning, daily, review, retro, 1:1s−5
Bugs and incidents, going by the last few sprints−4
Left for roadmap work26

Half the paper capacity is gone before anyone touches the roadmap, and nobody slacked off. If you plan against 50 when the real number is closer to 26, every sprint "slips" and people start to feel like the problem is them. The Scrum Guide makes the same point from the other side: the more the developers know about their past performance, their upcoming capacity and their Definition of Done, the more confident their forecast. For more on turning estimates into a conversation, see Agile Estimating and Planning: Treat Every Estimate as a Conversation.

Keep priority and order apart

"Most important" and "first" are different questions. A feature can matter a lot and still wait because an API it depends on isn't ready. A small compliance fix can jump ahead of an exciting product idea because the deadline for that risk is next month. A cleanup can earn a slot because every feature after it pays the cost if you skip it.

So the order on a roadmap mixes four things: value, risk, dependencies and what you need to learn first. When someone asks "why is my thing below theirs?", you can answer with whichever of the four applies. That answer is much easier to hear than "it's less important".

A better planning question

Swap "can we fit all of this?" for "if capacity is fixed, which outcome do we protect first, and what are we choosing not to do?"

That question has a well-known version. Basecamp's Shape Up calls it appetite: decide how much time a problem deserves, then shape the work to fit. In their words, "Estimates start with a design and end with a number. Appetites start with a number and end with a design." They call the principle "fixed time, variable scope" (Set Boundaries). Scrum lands in a similar place inside a sprint: the goal holds steady and the scope gets renegotiated with the Product Owner as the team learns more.

Say no without making it personal

A "not now" shouldn't mean the idea is bad, the person asking is unreasonable or the team isn't trying. Usually it means the team has hit a limit. There's only so much attention, review time and release risk a team can carry at once. Saying which limit you hit keeps the relationship intact, because now you're talking about a choice and nobody has to defend themselves.

One habit makes this much easier: write the cost next to every change. If an urgent item comes in, what goes out? If nothing goes out, which bar drops? Less testing, thinner docs, more evenings? A plan that keeps absorbing new work without naming what got pushed aside only looks flexible. The debt is still there, it just moved into people's evenings. Writing these trade-offs down where the team can find them later is exactly what a decision log is for.

Check the plan every week, while it's still small

Capacity talks go better when they're routine. If the only time anyone looks at the roadmap is during a crisis, every change feels like a fight. A weekly check can take fifteen minutes and five questions:

  • What changed since last week?
  • What did we learn that the plan doesn't know yet?
  • Which risk got bigger?
  • Which card should move, and what does that move cost?
  • Which decision needs a stakeholder before next week?

Do this regularly and the roadmap stays a working document instead of a museum piece. Product and engineering also get into the habit of updating the plan before reality turns into a surprise.

It takes some humility. The team admits it can't do everything at once, treats focus as a limited resource, and accepts that moving a card is sometimes the responsible call. Good delivery still changes the plan. What it protects is the outcome that matters.

Try this week

  • Fill in the capacity table above for your next sprint with your own numbers, and compare the last line with what you usually plan.
  • For the top three items on the roadmap, write down whether each one is there for value, risk, a dependency or learning.
  • Next time urgent work comes in, write what goes out in the same message.
  • Book a fifteen-minute weekly roadmap check with the five questions above.

Good place to start: list the work nobody put on the roadmap but everyone is already doing. That list is usually the first honest line of the next plan.

faqs.q: Why does a team never seem to finish what the roadmap planned?
faqs.a: Usually because the plan counts paper capacity. Story points and velocity only cover ticketed work. Support, code review, meetings, onboarding, incidents and context switching eat a large share of every sprint. Google's SRE book caps operational work at 50% of each SRE's time and reports an average near 33%. Count that work before you plan.

faqs.q: What's the difference between priority and sequence on a roadmap?
faqs.a: Priority is how much something matters. Sequence is when it makes sense to do it. A high-value feature can wait for a dependency, a small compliance fix can jump ahead because its deadline is close, and a cleanup can go first because every later feature pays for skipping it. Roadmap order mixes value, risk, dependencies and what you need to learn first.

faqs.q: How do you say no to a roadmap request without damaging the relationship?
faqs.a: Name the constraint instead of judging the idea. Say which limit the team hit, such as review time, release risk or people on leave, and write the cost next to the change: if this comes in, what goes out? That keeps the conversation about a choice, and nobody has to defend themselves.

faqs.q: How often should a team revisit its roadmap?
faqs.a: A short weekly check works well. Fifteen minutes and five questions: what changed, what did we learn, which risk grew, which card should move and at what cost, and which decision needs a stakeholder before next week. Regular checks keep the plan current and make changes feel routine instead of like a crisis.
